summary: Proposes a simple HTTP extension using a new Meter header, so caches can report how many times a page was used, and origin servers can limit how many times a cached copy may be served. Publishers can then still count visits despite caching.

plainLanguage.summary: When a copy of a newspaper is kept in a shared box, the paper still wants to know how many people read it. This lets the box send back a tally.

questions: how can caches report page view counts
what is the meter header in http
how do caches report usage counts to servers
subtitle: How web caches can report page-view counts to publishers, and how publishers can cap how often a cached copy is reused.

tldr.problem: Publishers who want to count visits often turn caching off with 'cache-busting', which wastes network traffic and adds delay for everyone.
tldr.mechanism: A new hop-by-hop Meter header lets a proxy volunteer to count uses of a cached response and report the totals upstream, and lets the origin server limit how many times the cached copy may be used before it is revalidated.
tldr.outcome: Servers can get a best-efforts approximation of usage while caches keep working. It is optional, and the RFC itself warns that it gives little benefit unless both proxies and servers deploy it widely.

today: RFC 2227 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is optional, and the text itself says it would give little benefit unless both proxies and servers deployed it widely.

sections.title: Why Hit-Metering Exists
sections.content:
Content providers want to know how often their content is accessed. To get that, some servers use cache-busting: techniques meant to stop responses being cached at all, such as setting immediate expiration dates or sending Cache-control: private. The RFC notes that it is unknown exactly how common this is.

The model borrows from print publishing. A publisher counts copies and estimates how many people read each one at least once; it does not try to count re-reads. The results are not exact but are still useful.

The RFC is explicit about its scope. The design is optional, proxy-centered (end clients are not involved), solely a performance optimization, best-efforts and neutral with respect to privacy. Its listed limitations are that it helps little if it is not widely deployed in both proxies and servers, and that it might reduce the pressure to adopt more complete solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: Websites like to count visitors, so they stop helpers from keeping copies of pages. That makes everything slower. This idea lets the helpers keep copies and still do the counting.

sections.title: The Metering Subtree
sections.content:
The design adds one new header, Meter, used in both requests and responses. It adds two features: hit-metering, where an origin server obtains reasonably accurate counts of uses of a resource via a proxy cache or a hierarchy of caches, and usage-limiting, where the server controls how many times a cached response may be used before revalidation.

Negotiation happens hop by hop, not end to end. The proxies that agree to take part form a metering subtree, rooted at the origin server. The Meter header MUST always be protected by a Connection header, so a message carrying it contains Connection: meter. It MUST NOT be sent to, or accepted from, a client whose version is lower than HTTP/1.1, because such a proxy might not handle the Connection header properly.

When a proxy forwards a metered response to a client outside the subtree, it MUST omit the Meter header and MUST add Cache-control: s-maxage=0. That forces proxies below the subtree to check with a subtree member on every request. No proxy has to implement any of this, but a proxy that sends Meter in a request MUST meet every requirement of the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the helpers who say 'I will keep count' join the counting team. Anyone outside the team has to ask a team member every single time, so no visit slips by uncounted.

sections.title: The Meter Header and Its Directives
sections.content:
A Meter header carries zero or more directives, much like Cache-control. Several Meter headers may be combined into one, for example Meter: max-uses=3, max-reuses=10, do-report. There are three kinds of directive.

  • Request directives from a proxy: will-report-and-limit, wont-report and wont-limit.
  • Response directives from a server: max-uses, max-reuses, do-report, dont-report, timeout and wont-ask.
  • Report directive from a proxy: count=NNN/MMM.

An empty Meter header in a request means will-report-and-limit. An empty one in a response, or any Meter header without dont-report or wont-ask, means do-report. To save space, every directive also has a one-letter abbreviated form, and all implementations MUST support both forms. The two forms may be mixed in the same header.
sections.plainLanguage: The Meter header is a short note passed between helpers and the website. The note says things like 'I will count', 'please count', or 'here is my count so far'.

sections.title: Negotiating Metering and Limits
sections.content:
A proxy starts by sending one of the request directives to the next-hop server. A proxy unwilling either to obey usage limits or to send usage reports MUST NOT send a Meter header at all. An origin server not interested simply ignores the header.

If the server wants metering, it answers with response directives. do-report says the proxy MUST send usage reports; dont-report says it SHOULD NOT. timeout=NNN sets a limit of NNN minutes from the time the response was originated: if the proxy has a non-zero hit count when it expires, it MUST send a report at or before that time. max-uses=NNN and max-reuses=NNN cap the number of uses and reuses for all proxies in the subtree taken together. When a proxy has used up its allowance it MUST revalidate with a conditional request before answering again.

A server MUST NOT ask a proxy to do something the proxy has not offered to do. A proxy receiving a Meter response MUST either obey it or revalidate on every access, acting as if the response included Cache-control: s-maxage=0. A server that never wants to be asked can send wont-ask, and the proxy SHOULD remember this for up to 24 hours.

A proxy may divide a usage limit among its children however it likes. The RFC's example is a proxy P3 that receives max-uses=10 and could keep all of it, passing on max-uses=0, or split it, passing on max-uses=5.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper says what it is willing to do. The website then asks for only those things, such as 'count visits' or 'only show this copy three more times before checking with me'.

sections.title: Counting Uses and Sending Reports
sections.content:
A use of a cached response happens when the proxy returns its stored copy with a 200, 203 or 206 status (206 only if it contains byte 0 of the entity). A reuse is a 304 (Not Modified) answer to a conditional request. The response the proxy sends right after fetching a new copy from the server is not counted as a use. HEAD requests are not counted.

A proxy that agreed to hit-meter keeps two counters per cached response, set to 0 when it first stores it. It reports them as Meter: count=NNN/MMM, uses first and reuses second. A proxy SHOULD NOT send count=0/0.

Reports MUST ride on a conditional request, because the conditional header tells the origin server which instance of the resource is being counted. Proxies MUST NOT change that header when forwarding. A proxy MUST send a report when it forwards a conditional GET or HEAD for a client, when it revalidates because max-uses was exceeded, when a metering timeout expires with a non-zero count, and when it is about to forget a non-zero count. In the last two cases the report goes in a conditional HEAD request, which need not be retried but SHOULD be.

When a request arrives that already carries a count, the proxy adds its own counts to it before forwarding. Range requests count only if they return byte 0. Separate counts are kept for each combination of headers named in a Vary header, which lets a server split statistics by request pattern.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper keeps a tally on a sticky note. When it next talks to the website, it passes along the tally and starts a fresh note, so nobody counts the same visit twice.

sections.title: A Complete Exchange
sections.content:
The RFC walks through the common case: hit-metering without usage-limiting. A proxy forwards a client's request with Connection: Meter, implicitly offering will-report-and-limit. The server's 200 OK carries Connection: meter, which implicitly requires do-report, and Cache-control: max-age=3600.

The proxy answers the client with the response plus proxy-mustcheck, since it does not know whether the client is an end system or a proxy that does no metering. Later clients are served from the cache. After an hour the proxy revalidates with If-None-Match and Meter: count=1/0, reporting the one use it did not forward. When it finally drops the entry, it sends a conditional HEAD with another count=1/0.

The RFC also shows a server that wants usage limits but no counts: Meter: max-uses=3, max-reuses=6, dont-report, or in abbreviated form Meter:u=3,r=6,e. To keep HTTP/1.0 caches from storing the response, a server can add an old Expires date, which HTTP/1.1 caches ignore in favour of max-age.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper serves copies to visitors and writes down how many it handed out. When it checks in with the website, or throws the copy away, it reports the number.

sections.title: Trust, Cheating and Privacy
sections.content:
The main worry is trust. A malicious proxy could report a large number of hits on a page and perhaps cause a large payment from an advertiser to a content provider. To help, a proxy may relay counts from outbound proxies only when they have authenticated using Proxy-Authorization or are on a list of approved proxies.

Usage limits cannot be enforced against a proxy that is willing to cheat, one that offers to limit usage and then ignores the directive.

On privacy, the RFC concludes that the design appears to reveal no more about individual users than existing HTTP/1.1 features such as Cache-control: s-maxage=0. It adds that the conflict between user anonymity and a server's wish for demographic information cannot be resolved by purely technical means.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky helper could tell the website a made-up big number to get someone paid. The website has to decide which helpers it trusts.

items.label: will-report-and-limit
items.desc: Proxy will send usage reports and obey usage limits.

items.label: wont-report
items.desc: Proxy obeys limits but sends no reports.

items.label: wont-limit
items.desc: Proxy sends reports but does not obey limits.

items.label: count=NNN/MMM
items.desc: Uses and reuses since the last report.

items.label: max-uses=NNN
items.desc: Upper limit on uses for the whole subtree.

items.label: max-reuses=NNN
items.desc: Upper limit on reuses for the whole subtree.

items.label: dont-report
items.desc: Proxy SHOULD NOT send usage reports.

items.label: timeout=NNN
items.desc: Report due NNN minutes after the response originated.

items.label: wont-ask
items.desc: Proxy SHOULD NOT send Meter headers to this server.
